title: Rolling windows
objectives: Compute rolling means and annualised rolling volatility.
Build a moving average signal that trades only on what it knew.

screens.title: A window that slides
screens.prose: Twelve closes of one stock, in £. The shaded band covers 3 days. The second line plots the mean of the closes inside the band, on the band's last day. Slide the band along.
screens.question: How does the 3-day mean line move compared with the price?

options.text: It is smoother, and it turns after the price turns
It turns before the price does
options.why: Each point averages closes already seen, so it can only follow a turn, never lead it.

options.text: It is the price moved one day later
options.why: Slide to 10 April: the price jumps 0.26, but the mean moves only 0.07.

options.text: It stays flat while the price moves
options.why: The mean changes every day, as one close leaves the band and a new one enters.

hints.text: Watch both lines around 9 and 10 April, where the price dips and jumps.
Each day the mean changes by (new close − dropped close) / 3, so one sharp move is shared out.

feedback.correct: It smooths the price and lags behind it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two lines at a sharp move.

explain.text: Each point is the mean of the last 3 closes, today included. One big move is shared with two older closes, so the line is smoother. It can only react after the price has moved, so it lags.

screens.title: Rolling windows
screens.prose:
What you slid is a **rolling window**. pandas computes the mean in every window at once.

```python
ma = df["close"].rolling(3).mean()
```
screens.question: What is `ma` on 2024-04-08? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: A 3-day window that ends on 8 April.
It holds 4, 5 and 8 April: 12.31, 12.48 and 12.62.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the 3 closes ending on 8 April, that day included.

byKey.before: You averaged the 3 days before 8 April. The window ends on 8 April and includes its close.
byKey.centred: You centred the window on 8 April. `rolling` looks back only: 8 April is the window's last day.
byKey.two: That is 8 April's close with 5 April's. A window of 3 holds three closes.

explain.text: `rolling(3)` labels each window by its last day. On 8 April it holds 4, 5 and 8 April, so the mean is $(12.31 + 12.48 + 12.62) / 3 = 12.47$. Weekends do not count: the window is 3 rows.

screens.title: The first few rows
screens.prose:
Now a 5-day window over all twelve closes.

```python
ma5 = df["close"].rolling(5).mean()
print(ma5.isna().sum())
```
screens.question: What does it print?

widget.label: Value printed
widget.accept: 4: the first 4 days have fewer than 5 closes behind them.

hints.text: A 5-day mean needs 5 closes.
On 5 April only 4 closes exist so far.
The first full window ends on the 5th row, so rows 1 to 4 are NaN.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the days before a full 5-day window exists.

byKey.five: The 5th day already has 5 closes: itself and the 4 before. Only the first 4 rows are short.
byKey.zero: `rolling` does not average a partial window. Until 5 closes exist, the result is NaN.
byKey.eight: That counts the full windows. The NaN rows are the ones without a full window: 12 − 8 = 4.

explain.text: A window of $n$ needs $n$ rows, so the first $n - 1$ results are NaN. Here the 5-day mean starts on 8 April. Passing `min_periods=1` would average partial windows instead.

screens.title: Rolling volatility
screens.prose:
The standard deviation of returns over a window is a **rolling volatility**.

```python
vol = df["close"].pct_change().rolling(3).std()
print(vol.isna().sum())
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: That counts only the window. `pct_change` already made the first row NaN, so the first full window of returns ends one day later.
That counts only the missing first return. A window of 3 returns adds two more NaN rows.
`std` does not skip a short window. Both the first return and the first two windows are NaN.

hints.text: Two steps each lose rows at the top.
`pct_change` loses 1 row. `rolling(3)` then needs 3 returns.
The first 3 returns end on the 4th row, so 3 rows are NaN.

feedback.correct: 1 from the return, then 2 from the window.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the NaN rows each step adds.

explain.text: The first return is NaN, so the first 3 real returns end on the 4th row. That leaves $1 + (3 - 1) = 3$ NaN rows. NaN rows from each step add up.

screens.title: From daily to annual
screens.prose:
A daily standard deviation is scaled to a year by $\sqrt{252}$, the number of trading days. Variances add over independent days, so the standard deviation grows with the square root.

```python
ann = vol5 * np.sqrt(252)
```

state.caption: vol5: the 5-day rolling standard deviation of daily returns

screens.question: What is `ann` on the last day? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Multiply the last value by the square root of 252.
The last value is 0.013987.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 0.013987 by $\sqrt{252}$, about 15.87.

byKey.times252: You multiplied by 252. That scales a variance; a standard deviation scales by $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.month: You used $\sqrt{12}$, for monthly data. These are daily returns, so use $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.cal: You used 365 days. Prices only move on trading days, about 252 a year.

explain.text: Variance over 252 independent days is 252 times the daily variance. Taking the square root gives $0.013987 \times \sqrt{252} = 0.2220$, an annualised volatility of 22.2%.

screens.title: A signal that sees today
screens.prose:
A colleague holds the stock whenever it closes above its 3-day mean.

```python
ma = df["close"].rolling(3).mean()
pos = (df["close"] > ma).astype(int)
strat = pos * df["close"].pct_change()
```

In this stretch `strat` dodges both losing days.
screens.question: Why does it dodge them?

options.text: `pos` uses the same day's close, which already contains that day's return
Nothing is wrong: the mean only uses earlier closes
options.why: The window ends on today's row and includes today's close. So `pos` already knows today's move.

options.text: The 3-day mean is a good predictor of tomorrow
options.why: It looks that way only because each day's position is set after that day's move.

options.text: The NaN rows at the start remove the losing days
options.why: The NaN rows are on 2 and 3 April. The losses on 9 and 12 April are inside the stretch.

hints.text: When is `pos` for 9 April known?
It needs 9 April's close, 12.44, which already reflects the fall.
The return on 9 April is earned before that close is known. Shift `pos` by one day.

feedback.correct: Each day's position is set after that day's move.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which close each day's `pos` needs.

byKey.before: That is the misconception. The window ends on today's row and includes today's close, so `pos` already knows today's move.

explain.text: On 9 April the close of 12.44 is below the mean, so `pos` is 0, but that close is the fall itself. Hold yesterday's position instead: `pos.shift(1) * ret`. Over the twelve days the total falls from 0.0830 to 0.0002.

screens.title: Rolling, in one place
screens.prose:
Each window ends on its own row, today included.

$$\bar p_t = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} p_{t-k} \qquad \sigma_{\text{ann}} = \sigma_{\text{daily}}\sqrt{252}$$

```python
c = df["close"]
ma = c.rolling(20).mean()      # first 19 NaN
r = c.pct_change()
vol = r.rolling(20).std() * np.sqrt(252)
pos = (c > ma).astype(int).shift(1)   # no look-ahead
```
screens.question: `c.rolling(20).mean()` on 30 daily closes. How many values are not NaN?

options.why: You took 30 − 20. The window ending on day 20 is full too, so only 19 rows are NaN: 30 − 19 = 11.
The first 19 rows have fewer than 20 closes behind them, so they are NaN.
20 is the window length. Count the rows with a full window: days 20 to 30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first $n - 1$ rows are NaN.

explain.text: With $n = 20$ the first 19 rows are NaN. Rows 20 to 30 each have a full window, which is 11 values.

quiz.prose: A stock's daily returns have a standard deviation of 0.015.
quiz.question: What is its annualised volatility, using 252 trading days? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.times252: You multiplied by 252. Variance scales with time, so the standard deviation scales with $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.cal: You used 365 days. Use the 252 days on which the stock trades.

explain.text: Variances of independent days add, so a year's variance is $252 \times 0.015^2$. Its square root is $0.015\sqrt{252} = 0.2381$.

options.why: That is the default. `min_periods=1` averages whatever the window holds, even one value.
You divided by 3 every time. A partial window is averaged over the values it holds.
That keeps growing the window. It is capped at 3 values, so the last mean is (2 + 3 + 4) / 3.

feedback.correct: Partial windows are averaged over what they hold.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With `min_periods=1`, a short window still gives a mean.
